<reason>Side A wins by consistently framing the issue as prioritization and marginal investment, not abandonment of existing channels. It answers the depth objection with series-based depth over time, answers the incentive objection with flat-fee editorially controlled partnerships, and flips universal service by identifying youth as the group not actually encountering public service. Side B's budget, broken-funnel, and universal-mandate pressures are serious, but B repeatedly treats prioritization as abandonment and repeats per-engagement and visibility objections after A had directly addressed them.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 was decisive: its A1/A2 answers distinguish commercial saturation from public-service access and replace per-engagement pay with flat-fee commissions, then use low marginal cost and sequenced clips to blunt both the cannibalization and broken-funnel attacks.</best_rebuttal>
